content.title: About
content.content: Dried apples are whole fruits of the apple tree (Malus domestica) that have been dehydrated to a low moisture level. They retain the sweet‑tart flavor of fresh apples but have a more concentrated texture and aroma. Dried apples are commonly used in baking, muesli, salads, and as a convenient snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dried apples can be stored for up to a year when kept properly, making them a handy fruit reserve.
Sugar concentration is higher in dried apples than in fresh ones because water is removed.
Traditionally, dried apples were used in folk medicine to aid digestion.
They are often added to classic dishes such as porridge, compote, and pies.
The apple aroma persists even after long storage.

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Dried apples provide a substantial amount of dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Although some vitamin C is lost during drying, dried apples still contribute a useful amount of this antioxidant.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols in apples help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Fiber and potassium in dried apples aid in maintaining healthy blood pressure and cholesterol levels.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Natural sugars give a quick boost of energy.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Because the sugars are concentrated, dried apples should be eaten in moderation, especially by people with diabetes.

items.title: Apple allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to apples, ranging from itching to swelling.

items.title: Sulfite content
items.content: Sulfites are sometimes added to preserve color and may cause reactions in sensitive persons.

items.title: Choking hazard for children
items.content: Small pieces of dried apple can pose a choking risk for young children.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Dried apples can be eaten straight as a snack, added to muesli, yogurt, baked goods, salads, or used to make compote and sauces. Soaking them in water can re‑hydrate them slightly if a softer texture is desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried apples in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. For longer storage keep them in the refrigerator. Discard any pieces that show mold, off‑odors, or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Blueberry juice is made from ripe blueberries grown in temperate climates. The drink has a deep violet color, a sweet‑tart flavor, and a distinctive berry aroma. It is often pasteurized for longer shelf life, though cold‑pressed versions are also available.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Blueberries contain over 80 different antioxidants, including anthocyanins that give the juice its rich hue.
In the United States, blueberry juice is popular in sports nutrition for its potential muscle‑recovery benefits.
Traditionally, Scandinavian cuisines use blueberry juice in sauces for meat and fish.
The juice can be 100% fruit or blended with water or other fruit juices.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and vitamin C help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports eye health
items.content: Studies suggest regular blueberry consumption may improve night vision and reduce the risk of age‑related macular degeneration.

items.title: Reduces inflammation
items.content: Flavonoids in the juice have anti‑inflammatory effects, which can be beneficial for chronic conditions.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Polysaccharides and potassium contribute to normal blood pressure and a healthier lipid profile.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Small amounts of retained fiber support gut microbiota.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Commercial juice often contains added sugar, increasing calories and affecting blood glucose levels.

items.title: Berry allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to blueberries.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in individuals with gastritis or ulcers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Blueberry juice can be enjoyed chilled as a refreshing drink, used in smoothies, cocktails, sauces, or as a base for marinades. Choose 100% juice without added sugars to reduce sugar intake.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C in a sealed container. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days. Frozen juice retains its qualities for up to 6 months.

macaroni-or-noodles-with-cheese-and-chic.title: Macaroni with Cheese and Chicken or Turkey

content.title: About
content.content: This dish consists of boiled macaroni (or noodles) baked together with melted cheese and pieces of boiled or roasted chicken or turkey meat. The combination of carbs, protein and fat makes it filling and popular for family meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Macaroni originated in Italy in the 13th century and quickly spread worldwide.
Cheese used is often cheddar, mozzarella or processed cheese, which melts well and forms a creamy crust.
Chicken and turkey are lean protein sources frequently chosen for children's nutrition.
The dish can be prepared in the oven, a slow cooker or on the stovetop, making it very versatile.
In some countries a similar dish is known as “navy beans” pasta, but without cheese.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Macaroni provides sustained energy and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Protein from poultry
items.content: Chicken and turkey supply high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cheese contributes calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Both the pasta and the meat contain B1, B2, B6 vitamins that support metabolism.

items.title: Low saturated fat (when using lean meat)
items.content: Choosing chicken or turkey breast reduces saturated fat compared with red meat.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The combination of pasta, cheese and meat makes the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Cheese and ready‑made sauces can be high in salt, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or dairy allergy should use dairy‑free alternatives.

items.title: Gluten in pasta
items.content: Traditional macaroni contains gluten; gluten‑free pasta should be used for celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cook the macaroni al dente, sauté chicken or turkey pieces, combine with grated cheese and a splash of milk or cream, then bake for 15‑20 minutes until golden. Season with black pepper, paprika, dried basil or your favorite herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the cooked dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For freezing, portion into freezer bags and keep up to 2 months. Reheat with a little liquid to prevent drying out.

content.title: About
content.content: A sandwich made with regular peanut butter, regular jelly, and wheat bread (2319) is a classic American snack. The bread provides carbohydrates, peanut butter supplies plant protein and healthy fats, and the jelly adds fruit flavor and a modest amount of sugar.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first recorded mention of the peanut butter and jelly combination dates back to the early 20th century.
In the United States the sandwich is often abbreviated as “PB&J” and is considered a childhood staple.
Using wheat bread gives the sandwich a denser texture and adds extra dietary fiber.
Peanut butter became popular among athletes in the 1960s because of its high protein content.
Some U.S. schools consider PB&J a healthier alternative to sugary snacks.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Peanut butter provides about 25 % protein, helping to maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Source of healthy fats
items.content: Monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids in peanut butter support heart health.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Fruit antioxidants
items.content: Jelly made from berries supplies vitamin C and polyphenols that boost immunity.

items.title: Fiber from bread
items.content: Wheat bread adds dietary fiber, promoting normal digestion.

items.title: Peanut allergy
items.content: Peanut butter can trigger severe allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: The sandwich is relatively calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Sugar content in jelly
items.content: Commercial jelly often contains added sugar, which may be undesirable for diabetics.

items.title: Gluten in wheat bread
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should use a gluten‑free bread alternative.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The sandwich is easy to eat by hand as a quick snack, at lunch, or post‑workout. You can add banana slices or a drizzle of honey for flavor variation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep opened peanut butter and jelly refrigerated, and store bread in a dry place.

potato-boiled-from-fresh-peel-eaten-no-a.title: Potato, boiled, fresh, peel eaten, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Boiled potato is a whole tuber cooked in water without added fat. The peel is retained, preserving most of the dietary fiber, vitamins, and minerals. Potato is a staple food in many countries and is often used as a side dish or a base for other meals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Potatoes were introduced to Europe from South America in the 16th century and quickly became a major food source.
The peel of boiled potatoes contains more fiber, vitamin C, and potassium than the flesh alone.
Boiled potatoes are easily digestible and are often recommended in diets aimed at gastrointestinal recovery.
There are over 4,000 potato varieties, differing in skin color, taste, and starch content.
Boiled potatoes can be used as a base for mash, salads, soups, and casseroles.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C in the peel and flesh supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber improves digestion, promotes satiety, and supports gut microbiota.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The absence of added fat makes it suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Starch in boiled potatoes provides a steady release of energy.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Boiled potatoes have a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood sugar spikes in people with diabetes.

items.title: Solanine content
items.content: If tubers are damaged or sprouting, the peel may contain solanine, a toxic compound. Green areas should be removed.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: A small number of individuals may experience an allergy to potatoes.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boiled potatoes can be served whole, diced into salads, mashed without butter, or used in casseroles and soups. The peel can be eaten together with the flesh, especially when it is well‑washed.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store boiled potatoes in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 3–4 days. Do not leave them at room temperature for more than two hours to prevent bacterial growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Red pepper, cooked, is the mature fruit of sweet pepper (Capsicum annuum) that has been boiled until tender. Cooking retains many nutrients while giving the pepper a milder, slightly sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cooked red pepper contains a higher level of vitamin C than its green or yellow counterparts.
Heat destroys part of capsaicin, making the taste less spicy.
It is widely used in Mediterranean and Asian cuisines in soups, stews, and sauces.
Cooking can enhance aromatic compounds, improving overall flavor perception.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: A 100 g serving provides over 150 % of the daily value of vitamin C, supporting immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Source of vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, promotes healthy vision and skin.

items.title: Contains vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and neurotransmitter synthesis.

items.title: Provides dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Minerals: potassium and iron
items.content: Potassium helps maintain fluid balance, while iron is essential for blood formation.

items.title: Pepper allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to pepper components.

items.title: Sodium content when salted
items.content: If the pepper is prepared with added salt, consider its contribution to daily sodium limits.

items.title: Loss of heat‑sensitive vitamins with prolonged boiling
items.content: Extended cooking can reduce levels of vitamin C and other thermolabile nutrients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked red pepper can be added to salads, soups, stews, pasta, and pizza. It is also used as a puree or sandwich filling. Serve warm or chilled, optionally drizzled with olive oil, fresh herbs, or balsamic vinegar.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked red pepper in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer keeping, freeze in portion‑sized bags – it retains flavor and texture for 2‑3 months.
